an-upload-route-passes-a-filefilter.why:
OWNER DECISION 52's FIRST PREMISE BROKEN, in the form it would really arrive: somebody adding a filter to reject non-CSV uploads, which is a reasonable thing to want and has nothing to do with security on its face. Kills PREMISE 1 in `multipart-upload-exposure.inventory.spec.ts`, which is the point of writing it as an inventory over the whole api source rather than a check on this controller: the real hazard is a SECOND upload route, and a per-file check would say nothing about one.
AND THE FAILURE IS ON THE PREMISE, NOT THE FEATURE. The upload still works; what has become false is `scripts/audit-check.mjs`'s record that multer GHSA-q7qp-rjg7-q26m is NOT EXPOSED, which rests on this product containing no `fileFilter` AT ALL. Note the plant is a SYNCHRONOUS filter, which the advisory says is unaffected — and the test still fails, deliberately: the record does not depend on reading a filter correctly, it depends on there being none, because the next one may be async and nobody will re-read the advisory. This repository already shipped a multer acknowledgement whose reachability half was false for sixteen days.

an-upload-route-accepts-two-files.why:
OWNER DECISION 52's SECOND PREMISE BROKEN. Kills PREMISE 2 alone, leaving premise 1 green — which is why they are two tests rather than one assertion: they fail independently and name different things to fix.
`files: 1` is load-bearing for a reason that is easy to miss: the advisory's mechanism is a request ABORTED because one file was rejected while ANOTHER file's filter is still pending. One file cannot reach that state. Raising the limit to two re-opens the mechanism even though no filter exists today, which is exactly the kind of latent re-exposure a record with two premises is meant to catch.

the-upload-extractor-stops-finding-route.why:
THE NON-VACUITY FLOOR, PLANTED ON THE GUARD ITSELF — the one failure mode that would make all three assertions above pass while checking NOTHING, because each is a loop over an extracted set and an empty loop passes. A renamed Nest export, a broken balanced-argument reader, or a comment stripper that ate the call would all produce this state, and a clean nothing is indistinguishable from 'no upload route passes a fileFilter'.
CORRECTED FROM THE RUN: I predicted TWO failures and it kills ONE. The floor test holds both assertions, and `expect(sites.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)` fires FIRST, so the companion `toContain('legacy-import.controller.ts')` is never reached — the positive-assertion-fires-first shape this repository has already paid for. Both assertions still earn their place: 'found zero' and 'lost the route I know about' are different breakages, and the second is the one that catches a PARTIAL extraction failure, which the count alone would survive. It is simply not what this plant observes. This repository has paid for a measurement that found nothing and read exactly like a measurement that found no problem four times.

a-maker-checker-type-loses-its-word.why:
OWNER DECISION 53's SEQUENCING RULE BROKEN — one of the fifteen loses its word, which is the half-built state she named: a map covering fourteen of fifteen renders the raw MEMBER NAME for the fifteenth, and that is the defect batch eight was right to refuse. Kills the maker/checker totality test in `record-entity-types.test.ts`, which reads the member list out of `maker-checker-pairs.config.ts` rather than restating it — so a SIXTEENTH pair fails the same test on the commit that adds it, which is the only moment anybody will know which word is owed.
`PolicyChecking` is the one chosen because it is the one word that had to be SLICED rather than pointed at: the only string naming it calls it a DISCREPANCY, which a policy-checking record may not have.

the-two-screens-word-one-entity-differen.why:
THE DIVERGENCE DECISION 42 SETTLED FOR ENDORSEMENTS, ONE ENTITY OVER. `Complaint` is in BOTH closed sets — six of them are — so wording it one way on `/internal-controls` and another on `/sla-dashboard` gives a reader who sees both screens two names for one kind of record. That is «التعديلات» versus «الملحقات» again, and it is the reason the two maps are deliberately SEPARATE rather than merged: separate maps are total over their own sets, and the price is that they can disagree.
Kills `the two maps never give one entity two different words`, which exists for exactly this. Note what it does NOT kill: both totality tests stay green, because a wrong word is still a word — which is why agreement is asserted on its own rather than assumed to follow from completeness.

the-dpa-register-stops-naming-its-approv.why:
ITEM 4(a) REVERSED IN THE FORM IT WOULD REALLY ARRIVE — not by deleting the field but by sending the ID as the name, which is the tempting edit because it always produces something to render. On `/vendors/[id]` that prints «اعتمده 7f3a…» — approved by a uuid — on the record that makes sending personal data to a third party lawful at all.
CORRECTED FROM THE RUN, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE POINT. I predicted it would kill the Playwright assertion that the two-person row names its approver. IT KILLED NOTHING — `vendor-detail.spec.ts` stayed 7/7, because that spec MOCKS the endpoint and so supplies `dpoApprovedByName` itself. A mocked endpoint cannot drop a field the api dropped, which is a recorded lesson this repository has paid for before and which I wrote into the change and then predicted past anyway. So an api-side observer was added — `names the assessor and the approver, and never falls back to a uuid` in the service spec, asserting BOTH branches and that the resolve is BATCHED — and the plant now fails there by name. The Playwright assertions still earn their place: they are the only thing that sees whether the name reaches a READER. And note the budget does NOT move either way: that screen's counted identifier is the PRESENCE TEST gating the approve control, which never reached a reader, so `check:rendered-identifiers` cannot see this defect at all — register entry 134. The test is the only thing that can.
